pa.why.q: How do I use my own domain?
pa.why.a: Add a CNAME record for a name under your domain, pointing at the alias's address. Turn off any DNS proxy for it.
faq.ownDomain.q: How do I open an alias at my own domain?
faq.ownDomain.a:
Where you manage your DNS:

- Add a CNAME record for a name under your domain, such as app. Most DNS companies don't allow it on the bare domain.
- Point it at the alias's address: the Copy of its row copies exactly that.
- Turn off any DNS proxy and CNAME flattening for the record.
- Open your domain. HTTPS is set up on the first visit; if that visit fails, open it again a minute later.

The computer's access rules still apply there. The Hub can't see your DNS to check it. To stop, delete the DNS record first, then the alias: a removed alias's name can be taken by someone else later.
faq.portOrAlias.q: What is the difference between a port's address and an alias?
faq.portOrAlias.a:
A port's address is built from your project and computer, so it is long. An alias is a short name you pick, such as my-shop, that opens the same port.

Remove an alias on the Computers page, and its address stops working.
faq.whichPorts.q: Which open ports get a web address?
faq.whichPorts.a:
Each listed port has a kind:

- Web: a TCP port. It gets a web address, which carries HTTP (WebSockets included) and nothing else. The Hub does not check that the port speaks HTTP.
- Other: a UDP port, or a port number known for a service that is not the web, such as 22 (SSH) or 5432 (PostgreSQL). It shows "No web address".

A program that listens only on 127.0.0.1 or ::1 is not listed here. Make it listen on 0.0.0.0 to have its port listed.
faq.hoodyPorts.q: Why are some ports counted but not shown?
faq.hoodyPorts.a:
Hoody and the system run their own services on the computer, such as the terminal, SSH and remote display. Their ports are counted under the table instead of listed, and the Hub offers no alias for them.

Ports of Hoody kit programs are listed with a Hoody kit tag. The Hub offers no alias for them either.
faq.makeAlias.q: How do I create an alias?
faq.makeAlias.a:
1. In Aliases and domains, choose Create alias and type the port. Nothing needs to be running on it yet.
2. Keep the suggested name or type your own: 3 to 61 lowercase letters, digits and dashes, no dash at either end, not already in use and not kept for the platform.
3. Choose Make alias. The alias then points to that port.

Shortcut for a port that is listening: choose Create alias in the row of a Web port of your own program. The form opens on the Computers page for that port.

A port can have several aliases.
faq.aliasStopped.q: What happens to an alias when its program stops?
faq.aliasStopped.a:
Nothing changes for the alias: it keeps its name and address.

While nothing answers on its port, the address shows an error page instead of your program. Once the program listens there again, the address opens it again. You do not need to create the alias again.
faq.whoCanOpen.q: Who can open a port's address or an alias?
faq.whoCanOpen.a:
Unless access rules say otherwise, anyone who has the address can open it, with no sign-in.

To limit it, set access rules on the Computers page, in the computer's Permissions tab.

The same rules cover the port's address, its aliases and any domain of yours that points at an alias. A short alias name is easy to guess, so do not count on the address staying secret.
faq.httpsPort.q: Is the address HTTP or HTTPS, and what if my program serves HTTPS itself?
faq.httpsPort.a:
The address is served over HTTPS, and Hoody provides the certificate.

An address with http in its name, such as http-3000, reaches your program over plain HTTP on that port. The Hub's port addresses and the aliases made here work this way, so your program needs no certificate.

If your program serves HTTPS itself, write https in place of http in the port's address, as in https-3000. Its certificate is not checked, so a self-signed one works.

faq.whatIsProgram.q: What is a program, and what are Running programs and Apps?
faq.whatIsProgram.a:
A program is something your computer keeps running in the background, like a web app or a service. Stopping one does not delete it.

Running programs are services this computer keeps on, like a website or a bot. Apps are programs you open only when you need them.

Programs you add to this computer show up here, and Hoody keeps its own programs under System programs.
faq.systemPrograms.q: What are the system programs, and is it safe to stop one?
faq.systemPrograms.a:
System programs keep the computer and the Hub working. Stop or restart one only if you know why.

When the Hub knows what relies on one, its confirm says what stops until it runs again: Bots and the agent, Terminals and the apps that open one, Scripts and their runs, Schedules, Apps, Notes, Displays or Files; this page and every program here depend on the Hub's daemon. The confirm says you can start it again from this page.

You can view a system program's sandbox but not change it, and it has no alias.
faq.keepOrOnce.q: What is the difference between Keep it and Run once?
faq.keepOrOnce.a:
Keep it saves the program on this computer: start it when you like, or with the computer. It may also start as soon as it is added, and each program on this computer has its own name.

Run once starts it now and isn't kept; after it ends, its result stays readable for 10 minutes. The name is optional for Run once: leave it empty and one is made up.
faq.startDone.q: When does a start count as done, and what happens when a program stops?
faq.startDone.a:
A start counts as done once the program has kept running for the time you set (empty or 0 means 1 second).

- If it crashes in that time, the start failed.
- If it ends normally in that time, the restart choice decides: restart it after a failure, always restart it, or leave it stopped.

With a port, a start counts as done once that port answers; write the port in the command too.
faq.sandboxLimits.q: What does a sandbox limit, and what do the starting points do?
faq.sandboxLimits.a:
A sandbox limits what the program can reach: files, network and resources. Starting points:

- No network (it cannot connect anywhere or listen on any port)
- No outgoing TCP connections (it can still answer on its own ports; UDP is not covered)
- Read-only files (it can read but not change them; add folders it may write to)
- Resource limits (fills empty memory and process limits with 512 MB and 256, and gives it its own temporary folder)

To run it without a sandbox, leave it as it is.
faq.sandboxNetwork.q: What do the network choices and allowed ranges do?
faq.sandboxNetwork.a:
Connections:

- Any is no network limit.
- Limited listens only on its ports and opens outgoing TCP only to the ports you list.
- None is no network at all, only for programs without ports.

Ranges are IPv4, like 203.0.113.0/24, separated by spaces; empty means anyone. Visitors through the program's web address arrive with their own address, so a range can shut them out.

When "Let the computer's own connections through unfiltered" is on, connections from the computer itself and its network gateway skip the range and rate checks.
faq.sandboxApply.q: When do new sandbox limits take effect, and what does removing them do?
faq.sandboxApply.a:
Saving may restart the program if it is running and the change affects how it starts; a restart stops it for a moment and interrupts whatever it is doing.

- If it was running, the new limits apply from its next restart.
- If the program is turned off, the policy applies when it is turned on.

Remove sandbox removes the whole policy: the program runs without these limits from its next start.

A start, stop or restart still waiting holds sandbox changes until it is confirmed.
faq.maybeWentThrough.q: What if a change may have gone through?
faq.maybeWentThrough.a:
When the computer's answer is missing, a change may have gone through.

- Check reads the list, the saved policy or the restart's receipt again and never sends the change again.
- Stop tracking clears the note and releases the held change: do it only if you know the change did not go through; if it did, pressing the action again does it a second time.

A change sent from another page is checked or stopped on that page.
